case_name: Suraj Mal Kailash Chand and Others v Union of India and Another
petitioner: Suraj Mal Kailash Chand and Others
respondent:
Union of India and Another
Supreme Court of India

25 September 1981
W.Ps. Nos. 3334-3343 of 1981.
The Judgment was delivered by: SEN, J.
1.  In exercise of the powers conferred by Cl. 18 of the Rajasthan Trade Articles (Licensing and Control) Order, 1980 (hereinafter referred to as the Order), the State Government of Rajasthan, on May 23, 1981, with the prior concurrence of the Central Government, by a notification fixed the maximum limit of wheat to be possessed by a dealer at any time at 200 quintals. The petitioners who are dealers in foodgrains challenge the constitutional validity of the impugned notification as violative of their fundamental rights u/arts. 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Cl. 18 of the Order reads as follows:
"18. No person shall, either by himself or by any person on his behalf, store or have in his possession at any time any trade article mentioned in Schedule I and Schedule II in quantity exceeding the limits fixed -
(
facts: The State Government of Rajasthan, on May 23, 1981, with the prior concurrence of the Central Government, by a notification fixed the maximum limit of wheat to be possessed by a dealer at any time at 200 quintals.
The petitioners who are dealers in foodgrains challenge the constitutional validity of the impugned notification as violative of their fundamental rights u/arts. 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

This Court, in Krishan Lal Praveen Kumar v. State of Rajasthan 1981 Indlaw SC 476 has held that the impugned notification does not offend against the fundamental right guaranteed u/art. 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
issues: The constitutional validity of the impugned notification
Whether the fixation of maximum quantity of wheat to be possessed by a dealer at any time is arbitrary, irrational and irrelevant
Whether the impugned notification offends against the fundamental right guaranteed u/art. 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
petitioner_arguments: The impugned notification fixing the maximum quantity of wheat permitted to be possessed by a dealer at any time is not only arbitrary, irrational and irrelevant but it is also an unreasonable restriction on the freedom of trade guaranteed u/art. 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
No guidelines have been laid down in fixing a limit of 200 quintals for a dealer at any time as to the manner of disposal of the stock of wheat in excess of the limit so fixed;
There is no distinction made between a wholesale dealer and a retailer in as much as the maximum quantity of wheat permitted to be possessed by them is the same, i.e. 200 quintals at any time;
The governmental action in fixing the maximum limit at 200 quintals displays arbitrariness as there is no differentiation made between different varieties and grades of wheat;

The fixation of the maximum quantity of wheat to be possessed by a dealer at any time at 200 quintals is also arbitrary because in the case of pulses, the maximum quantity of pulses permitted to be possessed by a dealer at any time is much higher.
respondent_arguments: The notification providing for the maximum quantity of wheat which may be possessed by any dealer at any one time is clearly designed to prevent hoarding of foodgrains and is certainly a reasonable restriction within the meaning of Art. 19(6) of the Constitution.

Once the State Government has issued a notification under Cl. 18 of the Order specifying the maximum quantity of wheat to be possessed by a dealer at any time, the machinery provisions of the Order come into play.
The fixation of the maximum limit of wheat permitted to be possessed by a dealer at any time is a purely governmental function.
court_reasoning: We are afraid, non of these contentions can prevail.
In view of the above observation, it is difficult to conceive as to how the contention based on Art. 19(1)(g) of the Constitution can at all survive.
If the governmental action is arbitrary or there is no rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved, it is liable to be struck down as violative of Art. 14 of the Constitution.

The fixation by the impugned notification of the maximum quantity of wheat allowed to be possessed by a dealer at 200 quintals at any time can not be held to be arbitrary merely because in case of pulses, the maximum quantity allowed to be possessed by a dealer at any time is substantially higher.
holding: The write petitions must fail and are dismissed.
There shall be no order as to costs.
If there be any order staying the operation of the impugned notification, it stands vacated forthwith and no formal order for vacating such stay need be issued.
cases_cited: Suraj Mal Kailash Chand and Others v Union of India
